title: Krishna eats at Vidura's house
hookLine: a prince's feast refused, a plain meal at a friend's house, and a paper plate
carry: prasadam: offered with love, returned as grace
tomorrow: a teacher asks his best student for his thumb. why?
last: PATIENT AS A TREE, UNDER WHOEVER PASSES.

lines: FIRST, A STOP AT THE ALTAR.
cards: Some families won't let anyone eat until everyone's at the table. Here's a kitchen with a stricter rule. A paper plate: rice, dal, a vegetable curry, something sweet.

Guests at a Hare Krishna feast eat it at long tables, elbow to elbow with strangers. But before any of them tasted it, the food made a stop somewhere else: the altar. And that stop changes what the food is.

teach.h: THE FIRST TASTE BELONGS TO KRISHNA.
teach.b: Devotees cook for Krishna first. Some devotee cooks won't even taste the pot, because the first taste belongs to him.
The food is offered at the altar with a prayer, and then it comes back as prasadam, a word that means mercy or grace. Why does the love matter more than the menu? The Mahabharata tells it.
Before the great war, Krishna goes to the Kaurava court as a peace envoy.

Prince Duryodhana lays out a royal feast for him, and Krishna turns it down. In paraphrase: one eats another's food when it's offered in love, or when one is in need; you have no love for me, and I am not in need.
Then he walks to the plain house of Vidura, the honest uncle at that court, and eats there.

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, SOME WATER.
teach.b: The Gita gives the rule in Krishna's own voice, in paraphrase: whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or some water, I accept that offering of love.
The next verse goes wider: whatever you do, whatever you eat, offer it to me. So the kitchen is a place of worship, and so is the dishwashing after.
And because prasadam is mercy, it's meant to travel, to feasts, festivals, sometimes the street, to whoever is hungry.

teach.h: COOK FOR KRISHNA, THEN FEED ANYONE.
teach.b: Hindus offer food at home shrines and temples in many ways; here it became the movement's habit: cook for Krishna, then feed anyone. A pot of dal on a dorm hot plate fits the list just fine.

how: In ISKCON temples, cooks prepare food for Krishna and offer it at the altar before it is served as prasadam at feasts, festivals and free meal programs.

s: in the Gita, Krishna asks for costly offerings
a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, offered with devotion, he accepts.
prasadam is food offered to Krishna first, then shared
offered at the altar, it comes back as mercy and is served to guests.
before the war, Krishna gladly ate Duryodhana's royal feast
he turned it down and ate at Vidura's plain house, where the food came with love.

games.q: your roommate's mom mails cookies her church group baked and blessed, 'for whoever needs one.' what might a devotee recognize in it?
o: food made as an offering of love and meant to travel past the family.
nothing much: blessing food only means something inside a temple.
a reason to keep them all, since blessed food is too special to eat.
games.why: prasadam is meant to travel, to whoever is hungry. a devotee might recognize that much; the prayers and beliefs behind the cookies are the church's own.

practice: Many Hindus offer food before they eat it, even silently at the table. If there's tea, coffee or anything to eat near you, hold it and smell it first.

Before tasting, set it down for a moment and say inwardly: this is for you, Krishna, or the name of God you know. If you don't pray, let the pause be a thank-you to whoever grew it, carried it and made it.
Then take one small taste, as if it had come back to you as grace.

wordCard.voice: The Hare Krishnas: a movement that cooks for Krishna first, and then feeds whoever comes.

orig.note: Sanskrit: prasada, grace or mercy; devotees call offered food prasadam.

carryVoice: Something to keep from Vidura's table: prasadam, offered with love, returned as grace. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Krishna's peace mission (he declines Duryodhana's feast, saying one eats another's food out of love or in need, and eats at Vidura's house)
Bhagavad Gita 9.26 (a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water offered with devotion is accepted)
Bhagavad Gita 9.27 (whatever you do, eat, offer or give, do it as an offering to me)
